rows.description: A teenager sets limits with phrases like I am not comfortable with that or I do not want to share that photo. Refusing is a right, and a true friend respects it, while pressure is a warning sign to tell a trusted adult.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: admiration, trust

rows.description: A teenager may promise to keep a secret or a pledge of loyalty to a friend. Promises to keep secrets about safety, harm or abuse should not be kept, and telling a trusted adult is the caring choice.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: trust

rows.description: A teenager may vow never to talk to someone again or swear to change overnight in a burst of emotion. Waiting a day before big vows allows real intention to settle.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager may feel first attraction and show it with blushing, teasing, texting or avoidance, and signals can be unclear. Respect means asking and accepting a no, and telling a trusted adult if pressure or unsafe requests appear.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: admiration, trust
related concepts: avoidance

rows.description: A teenager shows affection with emojis, streaks, memes or likes, which can be ambiguous. Meaning varies among groups, so asking directly is wiser than reading much into a like.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: affection

rows.description: A teenager shows admiration with likes, comments, hearts or a shared post. Such signals are quick and low-cost, so their sincerity varies; a specific personal message usually means more than a reaction count.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: admiration

rows.description: A teenager may look pleased yet squirm, deflect or joke when praised in front of peers. Discomfort at recognition is often about social exposure rather than dislike of the praise; a quiet private word may suit better.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: embarrassment

rows.description: A teenager learns that praise can be genuine, strategic or teasing, and checks whether it is specific, consistent and free of a request. These are cues only; motives cannot be confirmed from words alone.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: admiration

rows.subtype: Knowing when to involve an adult [Regulating]
rows.description: A teenager recognises that some worries, such as safety, self-harm talk or abuse, are too big to hold alone and tells a trusted adult even if a friend asked for secrecy. Care sometimes means sharing.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: anxiety, trust

rows.description: A teenager comforts a friend by listening, staying present and sending a supportive message. Fixing the problem or minimising it ("It's not a big deal") can feel dismissive; validation often matters most.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: resentment
